title: Young people distinguish trust in elections from distrust of politicians while seeking earlier voice and better civic preparation
source_unit: UK Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, Votes at 16 research: Executive summary, commissioned from Deltapoll
geography: United Kingdom; young people aged 14–17 across England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland

denominator.unit: young people aged 14–17 in a nationally representative survey; 32 focus groups also conducted

registration_knowledge.value: Awareness that people must apply to register was widespread but focus groups found uncertainty about what registration involves

government_understanding.value: A majority reported some understanding of how government works, but focus groups often found limited detailed knowledge

election_trust_politician_trust.value: Trust in elections was comparatively robust among survey respondents while focus-group participants generally expressed low trust in politicians

observations.method: Mixed-method Deltapoll research commissioned by MHCLG: nationally representative online/offline survey of over 3,500 respondents plus 32 focus groups.
observations.uncertainty: The executive summary reports patterns rather than full cross-tabulated estimates; survey and focus-group evidence are complementary but not interchangeable, and reported trust is not observed institutional performance.
observations.subgroup: Young people aged 14–17, nations of the UK, participants with different school, family, media, and political-experience contexts.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low trust in politicians does not necessarily imply rejection of elections; institutional reform may be evaluated through responsiveness and voice rather than generalized anti-democratic sentiment.

information_sources.value: Parents or adults at home, television, and social media were the three most common sources of political and current-affairs information

algorithmic_exposure.value: Focus-group participants often encountered political content through algorithm-driven feeds rather than actively seeking it; TikTok and YouTube were frequent platforms

cross_checking.value: Many participants expressed scepticism about accuracy and bias and described cross-checking against mainstream news

school_preparation.value: Strong majorities supported more teaching about voting, elections, and politics, while fewer than half reported school or college support that helped them feel ready to vote

observations.method: Mixed-method survey and focus groups on political information, reliability judgments, and preparation for voting.
observations.uncertainty: The source does not establish which information source caused knowledge, trust, or participation; reported cross-checking may reflect selective recall or group discussion dynamics.
observations.subgroup: Young people receiving political information through families, schools, television, social platforms, and different national education systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Algorithmic exposure can increase incidental political contact while skepticism and cross-checking may provide practical resilience if reliable alternatives are accessible.

observations.period: 2026; attitudes toward votes at 16 and wider participation

denominator.unit: survey respondents aged 14–17 across the four UK nations

voice_in_england.value: In England, more than half believed voting at 16 would make their voice matter more, compared with about a third who believed it would not

voice_in_wales_scotland.value: In Wales and Scotland, where voting at 16 applies in some elections, more than two thirds believed extending the franchise would increase their sense of influence

participation.value: School debates or mock elections were the most common wider political activity at around one third; sustained campaigning or activism was rare and issue-specific

readiness_tension.value: Focus groups combined support for earlier voting with concern about peer knowledge, readiness, and susceptibility to external influence

observations.method: Cross-national survey comparison supplemented by focus groups, with existing voting-at-16 arrangements considered in interpretation.
observations.uncertainty: Support and perceived influence are attitudes, not turnout or durable participation; national differences may reflect institutions, prior experience, question context, or composition.
observations.subgroup: Young people in England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland; those with and without prior exposure to elections in which 16- and 17-year-olds can vote.
observations.counterinterpretation: Earlier voting rights may increase perceived voice without automatically resolving civic-knowledge, information-quality, or responsiveness gaps.

denominator.unit: survey respondents aged 14–17 across the four UK nations

accepted_id_or_bank_card.value: In Great Britain, the overwhelming majority possessed at least one tested accepted form of identification or a physical bank card

england_id_or_bank_card.unit: percent of respondents aged 14–15 and 16–17 in England with at least one tested accepted ID or physical bank card

northern_ireland_accepted_id.value: 76% of 14–15 year-olds and 78% of 16–17 year-olds in Northern Ireland had an ID from the accepted list

alternative_id_awareness.value: Awareness of Voter Authority Certificates and especially Electoral Identity Cards was limited

observations.method: Survey questions on identity ownership and awareness of voter-identification routes, interpreted alongside different accepted-ID rules across UK nations.
observations.uncertainty: Possessing an ID or bank card does not establish that a young person can navigate registration, polling, or accepted-ID rules; the tested forms and national rules differ.
observations.subgroup: Young people aged 14–17 across the four nations, including groups with different access to national identity schemes such as the Young Scot PASS.
observations.counterinterpretation: Broad document ownership can reduce one participation barrier while information, registration, confidence, and institutional responsiveness remain separate barriers.

Executive summary of knowledge, trust, information, participation, and identification findings.

boundary: This record adds a youth political-socialization and voice layer. It combines a nationally representative survey of over 3,500 young people aged 14–17 with 32 focus groups; it is not a turnout study, causal evaluation of votes at 16, measure of future voting behavior, or proof that algorithmic exposure causes misinformation or distrust.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Executive summary reviewed for the mixed-method design, election and politician trust distinction, political information sources, school preparation, votes-at-16 perceived influence, participation, and identification findings.
